raw_response:
I’m old now, and there is only me in the house, so I won’t do anything too fancy this year. But I’ve farmed these 6.5 mu for many decades, and I know this land. Wheat-maize is still the safest way for me. Wheat gives me a steady harvest, and then maize follows right after, so even if one side is not ideal, I still have the other. Since I can irrigate from the well, I won’t cut water too much, but pumping costs money, so I’ll water at the key stages, not blindly. I have more schooling than many older farmers here, so I do look at the crop condition and timing, not only habit, but in the end I still go with a steady plan that matches my age, my labor, and what this land usually gives me.

For wheat, I’ll use a good local improved variety and sow in early October, not too late, so it can establish before winter. I’ll put most of the phosphorus and potassium, and part of the nitrogen, as base fertilizer, then topdress once around jointing if the stand looks good. I’ll irrigate about three times if the weather is normal: once after sowing if moisture is short, once at jointing, and once at grain filling if needed. For maize, the window after wheat is tight, so I’ll keep it simple: harvest wheat, clear the field fast, and sow within a few days. I’ll use hybrid seed, put some fertilizer at planting, then topdress once at the big flare stage. If rain is normal, one irrigation may be enough; if it turns dry, I’ll add another. I won’t overspend, but I also won’t save money in the wrong place and let yield fall.
